# Introduction

In this section, we show how to merge, collapse and reshape the various data structures within a given sweep of Next Steps to create a dataset at the cohort member-level (i.e., one row per cohort member). This is likely to be the most useful data structure for most analyses.

[Most Next Steps files already have one row per cohort member](https://cls-data.github.io/docs/next_steps-data_structures.html) and all files are linked with a single identifier, `NSID`, so combining data within a sweep is more straightforward than in, e.g., the [MCS](https://cls-data.github.io/docs/mcs-merging_within_sweep.html). There are two complications. First, information about cohort members' parents is stored in separate variables for the "main parent" and "second parent", so some work is required to create variables that summarise both parents or that relate to a particular parent (such as the mother). Second, a small number of files - notably the household grid - have more than one row per cohort member and need to be collapsed before they are merged with other data.

We use the following packages:

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Load Packages
library(tidyverse) # For data manipulation
library(haven) # For importing .dta files
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# setwd(Sys.getenv("next_steps_fld"))
```

# Data Cleaning

We create a small dataset that contains information from Sweep 1 on: the cohort member's sex and attitude to school, housing tenure, family social class (National Statistics Socio-economic Classification; NS-SEC), mother's social class, and the number of siblings living with the cohort member. Constructing and combining these variables involves restructuring the data in various ways, and spans the most common data engineering tasks involved in bringing together information from a single sweep.

The datasets we use in this tutorial are below. Note, the household grid is stored in a different subfolder to the young person and family background files.

```{r}
yp <- read_dta("safeguarded_eul/wave_one_lsype_young_person_2020.dta") # One row per cohort member
family <- read_dta("safeguarded_eul/wave_one_lsype_family_background_2020.dta") # One row per cohort member
hhgrid <- read_dta("household_grids/wave_one_lsype_household_grid_file_2020.dta") # One row per household member
```

We begin with the simplest variables: the cohort member's sex and their attitude to school. These are stored in a cohort-member level dataset already (`wave_one_lsype_young_person_2020`), so they do not need further processing. Below we rename the relevant variables and select them along with the cohort member identifier, `NSID`.

```{r}
df_yp <- yp %>%
  select(NSID, sex = W1sexYP, school_attitude = W1yschat1) # Retains the listed variables, renaming W1sexYP as sex and W1yschat1 as school_attitude

df_yp
```

Housing tenure is a characteristic of the household and is stored in the family background file (`wave_one_lsype_family_background_2020`). As there is one cohort member per family in Next Steps, this file also has one row per cohort member, and the variable does not need any further processing at this stage.

```{r}
df_tenure <- family %>%
  select(NSID, tenure = W1hous12HH)
```

Next, we create a variable for family social class using data on both parents. The family background file contains the NS-SEC of the main parent (`W1nssecMP`) and the second parent (`W1nssecSP`). As these are stored in separate *columns* (rather than separate rows), we can create a summary variable by operating across the columns. We first replace values outside the range 1-8 with `NA` (negative values denote various forms of missingness - for instance, `-98` indicates there is no second parent in the household). We then take the minimum of the two variables using `pmin()` (lower values of NS-SEC indicate higher social class). `pmin()` returns the minimum for each row; the argument `na.rm = TRUE` means that where NS-SEC is only available for one parent, that parent's value is used.[^1]

[^1]: `wave_one_lsype_family_background_2020` also contains a derived variable for family NS-SEC, `W1nssecfam`, which is instead based on the occupation of the household reference person. We create our own variable here to demonstrate the principle, which can be applied to any pair of `MP` and `SP` variables.

```{r}
df_nssec <- family %>%
  select(NSID, W1nssecMP, W1nssecSP) %>%
  mutate(across(c(W1nssecMP, W1nssecSP),
                ~ if_else(between(.x, 1, 8), as.numeric(.x), NA))) %>% # Values outside 1-8 denote various forms of missingness
  mutate(family_nssec = pmin(W1nssecMP, W1nssecSP, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% # Takes the lowest value of the two variables in each row
  select(NSID, family_nssec)

df_nssec
```

We next show a different way of using the main and second parent variables: reshaping the data from wide to long so that we have one row per *parent*. This is useful where we want to create a variable for a particular parent - in this case, the cohort member's mother. [The main and second parent are roles in the interview](https://cls-data.github.io/docs/next_steps-data_structures.html), and either could be the cohort member's mother, so we need to bring in information from the household grid to find out who each parent is.

The family background file contains the variables `W1mainres` and `W1secores`, which record the person number of the main and second parent in the household grid. Below, we first rename these variables so that they follow the same convention as the NS-SEC variables (a common stem, followed by `MP` or `SP`). We then reshape the data from [wide to long using `pivot_longer()`](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-tidy.html#sec-pivoting). The `names_pattern` argument uses a regular expression to split the variable names into two pieces: the stem (`"(.*)"`) and the suffix (`"(MP|SP)"`). The stem is used to name the new columns (`.value`) and the suffix is stored in a new variable, `parent`. The result is a dataset with two rows per cohort member, one for each parent.[^2]

[^2]: We use `zap_labels()` to remove value labels from the variables prior to reshaping. `pivot_longer()` stacks the main and second parent variables on top of each other, and will print a warning where their value labels are not identical. For more on reshaping data, see [*Reshaping Data from Long to Wide (or Wide to Long)*](https://cls-data.github.io/docs/next_steps-reshape_long_wide.html).

```{r}
df_parent <- family %>%
  select(NSID, W1HhIDMP = W1mainres, W1HhIDSP = W1secores, W1nssecMP, W1nssecSP) %>%
  zap_labels() %>% # Removes value labels
  pivot_longer(cols = -NSID, # Reshape all columns except NSID
               names_to = c(".value", "parent"),
               names_pattern = "^(.*)(MP|SP)$")

df_parent
```

`df_parent` now contains the person number of each parent (`W1HhID`). We can use this to merge in each parent's sex (`W1Sex`) and relationship to the cohort member (`W1R_1`) from the household grid (see [*Working with the Household Grid*](https://cls-data.github.io/docs/next_steps-household_grid.html)). We use `inner_join()` so that we only keep rows where the parent is found in the household grid (this drops, for instance, rows for second parents in families where there is no second parent). We then keep the rows for natural mothers (`W1R_1 == 8` \[Natural parent\] and `W1Sex == 2` \[Female\]). The result is a dataset with one row per cohort member whose natural mother was the main or second parent, containing the mother's NS-SEC.[^3]

[^3]: More detail on merging with `inner_join()` (and other `*_join()` variants) is provided in [*Combining Data Across Sweeps*](https://cls-data.github.io/docs/next_steps-merging_across_sweeps.html), as well as [Chapter 19 of the R for Data Science textbook](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/joins.html#sec-mutating-joins). Note, for many characteristics, the family background file already contains derived variables for mothers and fathers - in this case, `W1nssecmum` and `W1nssecdad`. The approach here is needed for `MP` and `SP` variables that do not have such an equivalent.

```{r}
df_mother_nssec <- hhgrid %>%
  select(NSID, W1HhID, W1Sex, W1R_1) %>%
  inner_join(df_parent, by = c("NSID", "W1HhID")) %>%
  filter(W1R_1 == 8, # Keep natural parents...
         W1Sex == 2) %>% # ...who are female
  add_count(NSID) %>% # Creates new variable (n) containing # of records with given NSID
  filter(n == 1) %>% # Keep where only one natural mother identified per cohort member
  mutate(mother_nssec = if_else(between(W1nssec, 1, 8), W1nssec, NA)) %>%
  select(NSID, mother_nssec)
```

Finally, we create a variable for the number of siblings living with the cohort member. This involves collapsing the household grid, which has one row per household member, so that it has one row per cohort member. `W1R_1` records each household member's relationship to the cohort member, with values between 13 and 17 indicating different types of sibling (natural, half-, step-, adopted and foster siblings). We count the number of rows that meet this condition using `summarise()` on a [grouped data frame](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-transform.html#groups) (`group_by(NSID)`) to ensure this is calculated per cohort member.

```{r}
df_siblings <- hhgrid %>%
  select(NSID, W1HhID, W1R_1) %>%
  group_by(NSID) %>% # Groups the data so summarise() is performed per cohort member
  summarise(n_siblings = sum(W1R_1 %in% 13:17), # Counts the number of rows where W1R_1 is between 13 and 17
            .groups = "drop") # Removes the grouping from the resulting dataframe

df_siblings
```

The same principles apply to the "hierarchical" files from Sweeps 8 and 9 - for instance, `ns8_2015_children.dta`, which has one row for each of the cohort member's children. Note, though, that cohort members only appear in these files if they have at least one record (e.g., at least one child), so some care is needed when merging the collapsed data with other files: cohort members who do not appear in the file should typically be assigned a count of zero, rather than `NA`.

# Merging the Datasets

Now we have cleaned each variable, we can merge them together. The cleaned datasets are all at the cohort member level. We begin with `df_yp` as this has all the cohort members participating at Sweep 1 in it. We then use `left_join()` to merge in other data so original rows are kept (and no more are added). As `NSID` uniquely identifies cohort members, we use `left_join(..., by = "NSID")` in each case.

```{r}
df_yp %>%
  left_join(df_tenure, by = "NSID") %>%
  left_join(df_nssec, by = "NSID") %>%
  left_join(df_mother_nssec, by = "NSID") %>%
  left_join(df_siblings, by = "NSID")
```

As noted in [*Combining Data Across Sweeps*](https://cls-data.github.io/docs/next_steps-merging_across_sweeps.html), `left_join()` will not throw an error if a cohort member appears more than once in one of the datasets - it will simply add rows. If you want `R` to enforce that each row is matched to at most one row in the other dataset, you can add the argument `relationship = "one-to-one"` to the `*_join()` function call.
